## Introduction

[Lab 1](class7_lab1.html){target="_blank"} showed k-means on simulated data:
Lloyd's algorithm step by step, bad starts, scaling, and choosing $K$. This lab
uses real patients. The question is one a clinician could ask:

> *If we give the algorithm only the lab results, and no diagnoses, does it
> find the thyroid conditions by itself?*

We know the answer for these patients, so we can check. In real unsupervised
work there is no answer key. This lab shows what to look at when you cannot
check.

The plan:

1. **Look at the data.** Five lab tests on very different scales.
2. **Preprocessing changes the answer.** k-means on raw, scaled, and
   transformed values.
3. **Bad starts.** Why `nstart` matters.
4. **Choosing $K$.** The elbow, the silhouette, and the gap statistic do not
   agree.
5. **Hierarchical clustering.** Four linkages, four different answers.

Every code cell runs live in your browser via webR, so you do not need to
install R. Packages and data load once when the page opens. Give it a few
seconds on first load. Click **Run Code** to run a cell. Run the cells in
order from the top, because later cells use objects that earlier cells make.

## A note on `caret`

In earlier labs, `caret::train()` fit every model. `train()` tunes a model
against an outcome, and clustering has no outcome. So in this lab, `caret`
does the **preprocessing** with `preProcess()`, the same tool that
`train(..., preProcess = ...)` used inside earlier labs. The clustering itself
uses `kmeans()` and `hclust()` from base R, and `silhouette()` and `clusGap()`
from the `cluster` package.

## The data: thyroid function tests

The data come from 215 patients at a hospital in Belgium (Coomans et al.,
1983). Each patient had five blood tests:

| Column | Test | What it measures |
|---|---|---|
| `RT3U` | T3-resin uptake (%) | how much thyroid hormone binding capacity is free |
| `T4` | total serum thyroxine | the main hormone the thyroid makes |
| `T3` | total serum triiodothyronine | the active form of the hormone |
| `TSH` | basal TSH | the pituitary's signal to the thyroid ("make more") |
| `dTSH` | TSH change after a TRH injection | how strongly the pituitary responds |

Doctors gave each patient a diagnosis from the full medical record:
**Normal** (euthyroid), **Hyper** (overactive thyroid), or **Hypo**
(underactive thyroid). We hide the diagnosis from the algorithm, and we use
it only at the end to check.

```{webr}
library(dplyr)

thy <- read.csv("data/thyroid.csv") |>
  mutate(diagnosis = factor(diagnosis, levels = c("Normal", "Hyper", "Hypo")))

labs <- thy |> select(-diagnosis)   # the five tests: all the algorithm sees

dim(thy)
table(thy$diagnosis)
```

150 of the 215 patients are normal. The two disease groups are small (35 and
30 patients).

### What a clinician expects

A clinician reads these tests together. In **hyperthyroidism**, T4 and T3 are
high, and the pituitary stops sending TSH. In **hypothyroidism**, T4 is low,
and the pituitary sends a lot of TSH to push the thyroid harder. The median
values per group show this:

```{webr}
thy |>
  group_by(diagnosis) |>
  summarise(across(everything(), median), n = n())
```

If k-means finds groups like these, it found real clinical structure.

### Scales and shapes

```{webr}
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)

labs |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "test", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "grey60", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ test, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "patients",
       title = "The five tests, on their own scales") +
  theme_bw()

round(sapply(labs, sd), 2)
```

Two problems are visible:

- **The scales are different.** The SD of RT3U is 13.2. The SD of T3 is 1.4.
  k-means uses Euclidean distance, so a difference of 10 in RT3U counts the
  same as a difference of 10 in T3. But 10 units of T3 is the whole range of
  the data.
- **TSH and dTSH are very skewed.** Most patients have a TSH near 1, and a few
  have values above 30. Those few patients are far from everyone else, and
  they pull the centroids toward them.

# Part 1 — Preprocessing changes the answer

### k-means on the raw values

`kmeans()` needs the data and the number of clusters. `nstart = 25` runs
Lloyd's algorithm from 25 random starts and keeps the best result. Part 2
explains why.

```{webr}
set.seed(42)
km_raw <- kmeans(labs, centers = 3, nstart = 25)

table(diagnosis = thy$diagnosis, cluster = km_raw$cluster)
round(km_raw$centers, 1)
```

The cluster numbers are arbitrary labels. k-means does not know which cluster
is "Hyper". Read each **column** of the table: which patients ended up
together?

The result is reasonable: cluster 1 is mostly hypo patients, and cluster 3 is
mostly hyper patients. But look at the centroids. The largest gaps between
them are in **RT3U** (90 to 126), the test with the largest SD. On the raw
scale, RT3U decides most of the distances.

### Scaling: give each test the same weight

`preProcess()` learns the mean and SD of each column. `predict()` then applies
them. This is the same step that `preProcess = c("center", "scale")` did
inside `train()` in Labs 3 to 6.

```{webr}
library(caret)

pp_scale <- preProcess(labs, method = c("center", "scale"))
z_scale  <- predict(pp_scale, labs)

set.seed(42)
km_scale <- kmeans(z_scale, centers = 3, nstart = 25)
table(diagnosis = thy$diagnosis, cluster = km_scale$cluster)
```

Now **all 150 normal patients** are together. But the hyper patients split
into two clusters (16 and 19). Scaling fixed one problem and showed another:
the skew. After scaling, the few patients with very high TSH are still far
from everyone, and k-means uses one of its three clusters on them.

### Fix the skew too: the Yeo-Johnson transformation

A log transform pulls in long right tails. But `dTSH` has negative values, so
we cannot take its log. The **Yeo-Johnson** transformation is a cousin of the
log (and of the Box-Cox transformation). It also works for zero and negative
values, and `preProcess()` picks the strength of the transform for each
column.

```{webr}
pp_yj <- preProcess(labs, method = c("YeoJohnson", "center", "scale"))
z     <- predict(pp_yj, labs)

set.seed(42)
km <- kmeans(z, centers = 3, nstart = 25)
table(diagnosis = thy$diagnosis, cluster = km$cluster)
```

This is the best of the three:

| Preprocessing | Normal together | Hyper together | Hypo together |
|---|---|---|---|
| Raw | 137 / 150 | 25 / 35 | 23 / 30 |
| Center + scale | 150 / 150 | 19 / 35 | 22 / 30 |
| Yeo-Johnson + center + scale | 145 / 150 | 33 / 35 | 24 / 30 |

**Same algorithm, same data, same $K$. Three different answers.** The
preprocessing is part of the model. Choose it with care, and report it.

### Do the clusters make clinical sense?

Profile each cluster on the **original** units, which a clinician can read:

```{webr}
labs |>
  mutate(cluster = km$cluster) |>
  group_by(cluster) |>
  summarise(across(everything(), median), n = n())
```

- One cluster has high T4 (16.4) and high T3 (3.5), with TSH near 1 and no
  TSH response. That is the **hyperthyroid** profile.
- One cluster has low T4 (3.1) and very high TSH (11.9), with a large TSH
  response. That is the **hypothyroid** profile.
- The large cluster (153 patients) has middle values on every test. That is
  the **normal** profile.

k-means never saw a diagnosis. It found the three textbook patterns from the
numbers alone. This profile table is the most useful output of a cluster
analysis. Without an answer key, it is the only way to decide whether clusters
mean something.

### A picture

Two tests carry most of the clinical signal: T4 (the hormone) and TSH (the
signal that controls it). We plot them on log scales. Colour shows the
**cluster**, and shape shows the **true diagnosis**.

```{webr}
thy |>
  mutate(cluster = factor(km$cluster)) |>
  ggplot(aes(T4, TSH, colour = cluster, shape = diagnosis)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  ggsci::scale_color_aaas() +
  labs(x = "T4 (log scale)", y = "TSH (log scale)",
       title = "k-means clusters (colour) vs. diagnosis (shape)") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The mistakes sit where the groups touch. A few hypo patients have only a
small TSH rise, and they look normal. A few normal patients have a high T4,
and they sit with the hyper patients. A clinician would call these
**borderline** cases. k-means must put each patient in exactly one cluster, so
it cannot say "borderline". The Gaussian mixture models in Class 8 can.

# Part 2 — Bad starts and `nstart`

Lloyd's algorithm always lowers the within-cluster sum of squares (WSS). But it
stops at the first point where no single step helps, a **local minimum**. Where
it stops depends on where it starts.

With $K = 3$, these data are easy: nearly every start finds the same answer.
With more clusters, there are more ways to go wrong. Run k-means 100 times
with $K = 5$ and **one** start each, and compare the WSS:

```{webr}
wss_one_start <- sapply(1:100, function(s) {
  set.seed(s)
  kmeans(z, centers = 5, nstart = 1)$tot.withinss
})

set.seed(42)
best <- kmeans(z, centers = 5, nstart = 25)$tot.withinss

ggplot(data.frame(wss = wss_one_start), aes(wss)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "grey60", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = best, colour = "#EE0000", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "within-cluster sum of squares", y = "runs (out of 100)",
       title = "K = 5, one random start per run (red line: best of 25 starts)") +
  theme_bw()

mean(wss_one_start > best * 1.01)   # share of runs at least 1% worse than the best
```

About **one run in five** stops at a worse solution, and the worst is about 9%
worse than the best. Each of those runs gives a different set of clusters,
and nothing in the output warns you. So:

- Always use many starts (`nstart = 25` or more).
- Always set a seed, so that you and your readers get the same clusters.

# Part 3 — Choosing $K$

Here we know there are three diagnoses. In real work you do not know $K$. We
try three tools and see what each one says.

### The elbow

```{webr}
wss <- sapply(1:8, function(k) {
  set.seed(42)
  kmeans(z, centers = k, nstart = 25)$tot.withinss
})

ggplot(data.frame(k = 1:8, wss = wss), aes(k, wss)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  labs(x = "number of clusters K", y = "within-cluster sum of squares",
       title = "Elbow plot") +
  theme_bw()
```

WSS always falls when $K$ goes up: more centroids always sit closer to the
points. So we look for the **bend**, the $K$ after which the gain gets small.
Here, WSS falls by 346 from $K=1$ to 2, and by 236 from 2 to 3. After that,
each step gains 70 or less. The elbow is at $K = 3$. But "where is the bend"
is a judgement, and different people see it at different places.

### The silhouette

The silhouette asks one question about each point: *is this point closer to
its own cluster than to the nearest other cluster?*

For each point $i$:

1. Calculate $a(i)$. This is the mean distance from point $i$ to all other
   points in its own cluster.
2. For each other cluster, calculate the mean distance from point $i$ to all
   points in that cluster. Find the smallest of these mean distances. This is
   $b(i)$. The cluster that gives $b(i)$ is the **nearest other cluster**.
3. Calculate the silhouette width:
   $$s(i) = \frac{b(i) - a(i)}{\max\{a(i),\; b(i)\}}.$$

The value of $s(i)$ is always between $-1$ and $1$:

- If $s(i)$ is near $1$, point $i$ is near its own cluster and far from the
  nearest other cluster. The point is in the correct cluster.
- If $s(i)$ is near $0$, point $i$ is at the same distance from both clusters.
  The point is on the border between two clusters.
- If $s(i)$ is less than $0$, point $i$ is nearer to the other cluster than to
  its own cluster. The point is probably in the wrong cluster.

To get one value for one clustering, calculate the mean of $s(i)$ for all
points. This is the **average silhouette width**. Do this for each value of
$K$. Use the $K$ that gives the largest average silhouette width.

Two warnings:

- The silhouette is not defined for $K = 1$. It cannot tell you "there are no
  clusters".
- The silhouette prefers clusters that are compact and well separated. A large
  value does not prove that the clusters have a real meaning.

`cluster::silhouette()` needs the cluster labels and the distance matrix:

```{webr}
library(cluster)

d <- dist(z)                     # Euclidean distances on the transformed data

sil_k <- sapply(2:8, function(k) {
  set.seed(42)
  cl <- kmeans(z, centers = k, nstart = 25)$cluster
  mean(silhouette(cl, d)[, "sil_width"])
})

ggplot(data.frame(k = 2:8, sil = sil_k), aes(k, sil)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2:8) +
  labs(x = "number of clusters K", y = "average silhouette width",
       title = "Silhouette: larger is better") +
  theme_bw()

round(sil_k, 3)
```

The silhouette picks **$K = 2$** (0.445), with $K = 3$ close behind (0.406).
What does $K = 2$ look like?

```{webr}
set.seed(42)
km2 <- kmeans(z, centers = 2, nstart = 25)
table(diagnosis = thy$diagnosis, cluster = km2$cluster)
```

$K = 2$ puts all the hyper patients **with** the normal patients. It finds
"hypo vs. everyone else". The hypo patients, with their very high TSH, are
the most separated group, so this split gives the most compact, best
separated clusters. It is a valid answer to the geometric question. It is the
wrong answer to the clinical one.

### Silhouette widths for each patient

The average hides detail. Plot $s(i)$ for every patient in the $K = 3$
solution, sorted within each cluster, and colour each bar by diagnosis:

```{webr}
sil3 <- silhouette(km$cluster, d)

data.frame(cluster   = factor(sil3[, "cluster"]),
           width     = sil3[, "sil_width"],
           diagnosis = thy$diagnosis) |>
  arrange(cluster, desc(width)) |>
  mutate(patient = row_number()) |>
  ggplot(aes(patient, width, fill = diagnosis)) +
  geom_col(width = 1) +
  facet_grid(~ cluster, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x",
             labeller = label_both) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Normal = "grey70", Hyper = "#E69F00",
                               Hypo = "#7B3294")) +   # diagnosis colours, not cluster colours
  labs(x = "patients, sorted within each cluster", y = "silhouette width s(i)",
       title = "Silhouette widths for K = 3") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank())

round(tapply(sil3[, "sil_width"], thy$diagnosis, mean), 3)
```

No patient has a negative width. The hyper patients have the smallest widths
(mean 0.29): they sit close to the normal cluster. This is why the silhouette
prefers to merge them with the normal patients. The plot also shows the
borderline patients from the scatter plot: they are the short bars at the
right end of each cluster.

### The gap statistic

The gap statistic compares the WSS of the data with the WSS of **reference
data that have no clusters**: points drawn uniformly over the range of each
variable. It is the same idea as a permutation test: build a "nothing here"
version of the data, and ask if the real data look different. $B$ is the
number of reference data sets. **This cell takes a while.**

```{webr}
#| timelimit: 300
set.seed(42)
gap <- clusGap(as.matrix(z), FUNcluster = kmeans, K.max = 8, B = 50, nstart = 10)

gap_tab <- data.frame(k = 1:8, gap$Tab)
ggplot(gap_tab, aes(k, gap)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = gap - SE.sim, ymax = gap + SE.sim), width = 0.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  labs(x = "number of clusters K", y = "Gap(K)",
       title = "Gap statistic with 1-SE error bars") +
  theme_bw()

maxSE(gap$Tab[, "gap"], gap$Tab[, "SE.sim"], method = "firstSEmax")
```

The rule from the slides (the smallest $K$ with Gap($K$) $\geq$ Gap($K+1$) $-$
SE) gives **$K = 1$**: "no clusters". The curve is almost flat. Gap(3) to
Gap(8) are all within about 0.02 of each other.

Why does it fail here? The uniform reference fills a box. These data are one
large group of normal patients with two small groups at its edges. Compared
with a box, the normal group alone already looks "clustered". The two small
groups then add little extra. The gap statistic works best when the clusters
have similar sizes.

### Three tools, three answers

| Tool | Chosen $K$ |
|---|---|
| Elbow | 3 (by eye) |
| Silhouette | 2 |
| Gap statistic (1-SE rule) | 1 |
| Medical knowledge | 3 |

This happens often in practice. Each tool
answers its own question about geometry. None of them knows what the clusters
are **for**. Use the tools to find a short list of $K$ values. Then profile the
clusters for each $K$ (as in Part 1) and choose with a domain expert.

# Part 4 — Hierarchical clustering

Hierarchical clustering does not need $K$ in advance. It merges the two
closest groups, again and again, until one group remains. The **linkage**
defines "closest" for groups of points:

- **complete**: the largest distance between a point in one group and a point
  in the other
- **average**: the mean of all such distances
- **single**: the smallest such distance
- **Ward**: the merge that adds the least WSS (the k-means criterion)

We use the same distance matrix `d` as before, so all four methods see the
same data.

```{webr}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 8
linkages <- c("complete", "average", "single", "ward.D2")
trees <- lapply(linkages, function(m) hclust(d, method = m))
names(trees) <- linkages

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for (m in linkages) {
  plot(trees[[m]], labels = FALSE, hang = -1, main = m, xlab = "", sub = "")
  rect.hclust(trees[[m]], k = 3, border = c("#3B4992", "#EE0000", "#008B45"))
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The boxes show where a cut into 3 groups falls. The trees have very different
shapes:

- **Single** linkage makes a long staircase. It adds one patient at a time to
  one big group. This is called **chaining**.
- **Complete** and **Ward** make compact, balanced branches.

Now cut each tree at $K = 3$ and compare with the diagnosis:

```{webr}
for (m in linkages) {
  cat("\n---", m, "---\n")
  print(table(diagnosis = thy$diagnosis, cluster = cutree(trees[[m]], k = 3)))
}
```

| Linkage | Normal together | Hyper together | Hypo together |
|---|---|---|---|
| complete | 147 / 150 | 24 / 35 | 24 / 30 |
| average | 150 / 150 | 15 / 35 | 24 / 30 |
| single | 150 / 150 | — | — |
| Ward | 136 / 150 | 32 / 35 | 24 / 30 |
| *k-means (Part 1)* | *145 / 150* | *33 / 35* | *24 / 30* |

- **Single linkage fails.** One cluster holds 211 of the 215 patients. The
  other two clusters hold 3 patients and 1 patient. A 3-cluster cut of a
  chained tree only splits off the last few outliers.
- **Ward is the closest to k-means.** This is expected, because Ward merges by
  the same criterion that k-means minimizes.
- Average linkage keeps the normal group whole, but it loses half of the
  hyper patients into it.

The choice of linkage is a modelling choice, like the preprocessing in Part 1.
It can change the answer as much as the choice of algorithm.

## Try it yourself

**1. Four clusters.** Re-run k-means with `centers = 4`. Which group does the
fourth cluster split? Profile the clusters on the original units (copy the
profile code from Part 1). Is the new split clinically meaningful, or does
k-means cut a continuous group in two?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_k4
set.seed(42)
km4 <- kmeans(z, centers = ______, nstart = 25)
table(diagnosis = thy$diagnosis, cluster = km4$cluster)

labs |>
  mutate(cluster = km4$cluster) |>
  group_by(cluster) |>
  summarise(across(everything(), median), n = n())
```

**2. Fewer tests.** A clinic often orders only T4 and TSH. Cluster with those
two columns only (use `z[, c("T4", "TSH")]`). How many patients does each
diagnosis lose, compared with all five tests?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_two_tests
set.seed(42)
km_two <- kmeans(z[, c(______, ______)], centers = 3, nstart = 25)
table(diagnosis = thy$diagnosis, cluster = km_two$cluster)
```

**3. Scaled only, then the silhouette.** Re-run the silhouette loop from
Part 3 on `z_scale` (centered and scaled, no Yeo-Johnson). Which $K$ does it
pick now? Compare with the table in Part 1: the preprocessing with the better
match to the diagnoses has the **lower** silhouette. What does this tell you
about using the silhouette to choose the preprocessing?

## Things worth remembering

- **Preprocessing is part of the model.** Raw, scaled, and transformed data
  gave three different clusterings. Always scale. Check for skew, and
  transform when one tail dominates.
- **Use many starts and set a seed.** One start can stop at a worse local
  minimum, and nothing warns you.
- **The tools for choosing $K$ often disagree.** The elbow, the silhouette, and
  the gap statistic each answer a geometric question. Use them to find a short
  list, then decide with the profiles and with someone who knows the domain.
- **Profile your clusters.** A table of cluster medians on the original units
  is what turns "cluster 2" into "hypothyroid".
- **Linkage matters.** Single linkage chains. Ward behaves most like k-means.
